title: Influence of strain rate on the mechanical behaviour of high-manganese TWIP steel tested using a flywheel machine
abstract: Abstract The present study investigates the dynamic tensile behaviour of a high-manganese austenitic TWIP steel (X45MnAl20-4) using a flywheel-based testing system, with emphasis on strain rate effects. Dynamic tensile tests with strain rates ranging from approximately 300 to 950 s −1 . The force vs. time signals were recorded during the course of tests. This allowed the true stress–true strain diagrams to be determined. It has been established that the propagation of elastic stress waves within the test stand construction caused oscillations in the  σ true -ε true  curves. The smoothing of these oscillations has been approached through the utilisation of a power function as an approximation. The influence of strain rate on the tested steel characteristics such as flow stress, plastic deformation work, and absorbed energy (SEA and VEA) was quantitatively evaluated on the basis of the obtained  σ true -ε true  curves. Microscopic observations confirmed that mechanical twinning is the predominant deformation mechanism in the steel studied, with increased twinning density and multisystem twinning under dynamic conditions. A comparison of the X45MnAl20-4 steel with other TWIP steels and DP steel has shown that it exhibits a competitive specific SEA value. This confirms its suitability for use in structural components operating under dynamic loading conditions. The findings of the study underscore the significance of accurate measurement data interpretation and selection of suitable correction methods when analysing the dynamic mechanical responses of TWIP steels by means of a flywheel machine.
journal: Archives of Civil and Mechanical Engineering

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Currently, new technologies [ 1 ], modifying existing technologies [ 2 ], and new materials [ 3 ,  4 ] that will produce products with increasingly better properties are being sought. To enhance safety and performance of structural designs in automotive engineering, it is essential to investigate how materials behave under extreme conditions [ 5 ] including dynamic loading [ 6 ]. Investigating fundamental properties such as flow stress under dynamic loading conditions is essential for evaluating the mechanical performance and energy absorption capacity of automotive components and road infrastructure [ 7 ] designed to withstand crash impacts. One of the main directions in modern material research is the application of advanced materials with improved mechanical performance under extreme loading conditions [ 8 ]. Among these, Advanced High-Strength Steels (AHSS) play a crucial role [ 9 ,  10 ], especially in the automotive sector, where they are extensively used for structural components of the car body that must ensure both crashworthiness and efficient energy absorption during impact events, which is described by specific energy absorption (SEA) [ 11 ]. Their application contributes significantly to the reduction of vehicle weight [ 12 ], which is a key factor in meeting stringent environmental regulations and maintaining competitiveness in the global market [ 13 ]. A particularly promising subgroup of AHSS is represented by austenitic TWIP (Twinning-Induced Plasticity) steels [ 14 ]. These steels demonstrate an exceptional combination of high strength and excellent ductility [ 15 ], and also the highest values of SEA [ 16 ,  17 ], making them suitable for dynamic applications. The superior mechanical behaviour of TWIP steels results from their unique deformation mechanism—mechanical twinning [ 18 ]—which becomes especially prominent under dynamic (high strain rate) deformation. This mechanism not only enhances the strain hardening capability of the material but also delays the onset of necking, leading to improved formability and energy absorption under rapid loading. The development of TWIP steels is driven by the desire to reduce weight using thinner walled components while maintaining the same level of safety and simultaneously reducing CO 2  emissions [ 19 ]. Consequently, TWIP steels are a strong candidate for critical safety components subjected to dynamic stress, such as crash zones in automotive structures [ 20 ]. Dynamic tests, such as high strain rate tensile testing of sheet-metal or bar-shaped specimens, provide a representative assessment of material performance under crash-relevant loading conditions. These tests simulate real-world conditions where materials experience rapid loading, such as in automotive crashes, aerospace applications, and ballistic impacts. By subjecting specimens to controlled dynamic loads, researchers can observe the material's deformation, fracture mechanisms, and overall behaviour under stress [ 6 ]. The dynamic mechanical properties and microstructures associated with dynamic plastic deformation are heavily affected by strain, strain rate, and temperature [ 21 ].

Analysis of the dynamic properties of materials can be based on various experimental techniques that utilize the split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) [ 6 ,  13 ,  17 ], the flywheel machine [ 22 ] or the flying wedge [ 23 ,  24 ]. Hybrid methods may also be employed, combining standard Charpy impact tests and numerical analyses [ 24 ]. All these methods involve applying a dynamic impact of a hitter or hammer to obtain the loading, at a constant velocity. However, the dynamic impact generates the clattering effect and propagation of elastic stress-waves in steel tooling that are registered during a test [ 11 ,  25 ]. These undesirable effects can strongly disturb the stress–strain characteristics obtained during the test. In flywheel machines, some unique design elements such as the large diameter wheel, pendulum systems, and specimen holding devices play a key role in generating and controlling the stress waves. The wheel's mass and rotational speed determine the energy imparted to the specimen, while the pendulum systems ensure precise application of tensile loads [ 22 ,  26 ] The integration of piezoelectric and gauge sensors within the specimen holding devices allows for accurate measurement of force and displacement, providing valuable data on wave propagation dynamics [ 25 ].

By examining the experimental results obtained from dynamic tensile tests on austenitic TWIP steels, papers demonstrates the critical role of device construction and data analysis system in shaping the force–displacement curves, analysis the data in the context of flow stress determination and designing the model of approximation the true stress–true strain curves for obtaining the real results with the correction for wave propagation behaviour. The findings underscore the importance of optimizing device design to achieve reliable and reproducible results in dynamic loading experiments. A relatively small number of publications are devoted to the very methodology of developing the results that are obtained during dynamic deformation tests on a flywheel machine.

Recent studies on the flywheel machine presented in this paper [ 27 ] were not focused on the deep analysis of acquired data processing. Typically, only raw measured data in the form of force–time diagrams were published [ 28 ] without attempting to model stress–strain curves. In this work, strain and stress values were determined with reference to the initial geometrical dimensions of the specimen.

This paper presents the results of dynamic tensile tests carried out on a flywheel machine in the context of investigating the effect of strain rate on flow stress and energy absorption for the TWIP steel. A test stand was used in which the energy stored in the flywheel is transferred using a hammer tup to a specimen fixed in a stationary holding device. In the results development stage, the methodology for determining  σ true -ε true  curves from the measurement signals recorded on the test stand for different strain rates was presented. For the determined  σ true -ε true  courses, the form of the approximating function was proposed, and its parameters were calculated. Absorbed energy values related to the unit of volume (VEA) and related to the unit of mass (SEA) were determined for the specimens tested. The microstructure of tested steel was analysed in terms of the strain rate impact on the twins generation process.

sections.heading: Preparation of material
paragraphs: The material for testing was high-manganese steel with the chemical composition shown in Table  1 , subjected to solution heat treatment from a temperature of 1150°C/2h and water cooling. The assumed chemical composition of the steel provided a single-phase austenitic microstructure (Fig.  1 ), which was consistent with the adopted assumptions. An average grain size of the tested steel was 260 μm and the hardness in the initial state was 149 HV2. On the base of thermodynamic calculations [ 9 ,  29 ] the steel exhibits 26.4 mJ/m 2  SFE value. sections.heading: Static tensile tests
paragraphs: Static tensile tests at room temperature were performed to determine mechanical properties and to obtain stress–strain relations that will be compared with dynamic characteristics of the tested steel. Tests were carried out according to the PN-EN ISO 6892–1 standard using a servo hydraulic MTS-810 material testing machine equipped with a digital control system TestSTAR II and TestWARE SX for precise test control and data acquisition. The engineering stress–engineering strain diagram is presented in Fig.  2 . Fig. 2 Engineering stress–engineering strain diagram for the tested steel under static conditions (strain rate of 0.001 s. −1 )

It was found that the tested TWIP steel exhibits high ductility (uniform elongation ca. 70%, total elongation ca. 80% and reduction of area ca. 50%) and quite high plastic capacity expressed by UTS/YS ratio = 2.1 (the ultimate tensile strength—587 MPa and the yield strength—280 MPa). Such a combination of great ductility and intensive strain-hardening behaviour is crucial for energy-absorption applications.

sections.heading: Dynamic tensile tests
paragraphs: A flywheel machine were used to conduct dynamic tensile tests (Fig.  3 ). To carry out the test, the flywheel (which has a high moment of inertia) needs to be accelerated to a given linear speed. When the required speed is achieved, the hammer tup (previously hidden inside the flywheel) is released and hits the anvil attached to the end of the sample. Fig. 3 Schematic representation of the flywheel machine
Dynamic tensile tests were conducted on cylindrical specimens with threaded ends (Fig.  4 ). Fig. 4 Geometric features of specimens used for dynamic tensile tests

A view of the test stand with the mounted specimen is shown in Fig.  5 . To control the flywheel speed and to measure the impact force, a dedicated measurement system is used. During the tests, the tensile force course as a function of time and the flywheel speed were recorded. The force was measured using a computerised system of strain gauge signal converters. The force sensor was mounted on a specimen holding device and one end of the specimen was attached to it (Fig.  3 ). The force impulse is generated by the hammer tup as it hits the anvil attached to the other end of a specimen. Tests were carried out for linear speeds of 7.5 m/s and 15 m/s and 25 m/s at room temperature. Two tests were carried out for each speed. Fig. 5 The flywheel machine;  a  the specimen holding device at the front and the flywheel with the hammer tup hidden inside,  b  the specimen with the anvil attached to the grip

sections.heading: Microstructure investigations
paragraphs: In order to observe the microstructure, metallographic samples were prepared from the deformed specimens. The preparation process included cutting, mounting, grinding, polishing, and etching in the 10% nital solution. Microstructural observations were carried out using an Olympus GX71 optical microscope at the Łukasiewicz Research Network–Institute of Non-Ferrous Metals. Figure  6  schematically shows the location from which samples for microstructural analysis were taken. The samples were examined along the axis of a specimen, in the region of uniform deformation of the sample which, as indicated by the previous work by the authors [ 30 ], corresponds to the true strain value of approximately 0.4. Fig. 6 Area of sampling for microstructure testing

sections.heading: Results of dynamic tensile tests
paragraphs: Photographs of the specimens after dynamic tensile tests are shown in Fig.  7 . Measurements of the gauge lengths show that, under dynamic tensile conditions the tested high-manganese steel exhibits a significant total elongation in the range of 70–79%. Due to the constant linear speed of the hammer tup during dynamic tension, the strain rate decreases during the test. Changes of the strain rate for the test conducted at the linear speed of 7.5 m/s are shown in Fig.  9 . Using the methodology presented here, the recorded force–time relationships were converted to the true stress–strain curves presented in Fig.  10 . Fig. 10 The σ true -ε true  diagrams obtained for mean values strain rate of 300 s −1 , 600 s −1 , 950 s −1

The  σ true -ε true  curves determined using the proposed methodology for specimens subjected to dynamic tensile loading were compared with the results obtained from the static tensile test (Fig.  12 ). The plot does not include the elastic range of deformation as well as the deformation range after the onset of necking. Therefore, the true stress in the presented uniform elongation region is in fact equal to the flow stress of the tested steel at specific strain rates. Fig. 12 Influence of strain rate on the true stress–true strain curves for the tested steel

On the basis of the  σ true -ε true  curves thus obtained, the values of the true stress (flow stress) corresponding to the true strain  ε true  of 0.4 were determined. The calculated values of  σ true  are shown in Fig.  13 . The flow stress values at dynamic loading conditions are higher of ca. 15–30% than the flow stress obtained during static tension. Fig. 13 The mean true stress (flow stress) values corresponding to the true strain  ε true  = 0.4

The selected curves obtained in this study are compared in Fig.  14  with selected previously published static and dynamic tensile test results carried out on specimens cut from TWIP steel with a chemical composition similar to that of the steel analysed in this work: X42MnAl21-3 [ 31 ], and X64MnAl15-1 [ 11 ]. The static tensile test results of the tested steel and the steel with slightly lower carbon content are very similar. Moreover, the hardening of the material shows almost a linear character. In the case of dynamic tests, the higher stress values correspond with the higher carbon content. In both cases, the hardening of the material shows a near linear character. In the case of dynamic tests, the hardening is less and less intense with increasing strain. This may be due to the much higher temperature rise of dynamically stretched specimens with respect to the temperature rise observed in static tests, which the authors analyse later in the article. Fig. 14 Comparison of true stress–true strain curves for specimens of similar steel grades, statically and dynamically tensioned on different test stands

Knowing the dependence of the true stress on the true strain, it is possible to calculate the work of plastic deformation  W p , which is equal to the area under the curve describing the  σ true -ε true  relationship (Fig.  15 ) multiplied by the volume of the specimen’s gauge length. Fig. 15 Area under the σ true -ε true  curve adopted for the calculation of plastic deformation work

The plastic deformation work and the energy absorbed by individual specimens are presented in Fig.  16  and Fig.  17 . It can be seen that increasing the strain rate resulted in an increase in both the plastic deformation work and VEA. Fig. 16 The mean values of plastic deformation work corresponding to the true strain  ε true  = 0.4 Fig. 17 The mean values of absorbed energy corresponding to the true strain  ε true  = 0.4

The obtained SEA values characterising X45MnAl20-3 steel for different strain rates were compared with data for other TWIP steels available in the literature [ 11 ,  16 ,  30 ,  36 ,  37 – 38 ]. Figure  18  shows the value of energy absorbed per unit mass, while Fig.  19  captures the value of energy absorbed per unit volume. This allowed the influence of not only C but also Al content to be taken into account as mass reducing factors due to their low density. Comparing the SEA of the tested steel with others with a similar carbon content of about 0.45%, it can be concluded that the absorbed energy value is at a similar level. Steels with a high carbon content such as the X48MnAlSi18-1 steel examined in [ 39 ] and the X55MnAlSi25-5–1 steel investigated in [ 36 ] exhibit a higher SEA value. The X1MnAlSi24-3–2 steel examined in the study [ 38 ] is distinguished by its significantly diminished energy absorption capacity. It has been demonstrated that high SEA values are obtained for steels with a higher content of carbon and aluminium in their chemical composition. This results in a significant reduction in density without any detrimental effect on strength properties. A seminal reference for consideration may be DP 600 steel [ 40 ], which exhibits the lowest absorbed energy per unit volume compared to TWIP steel, a result of its higher density. sections.heading: Microstructure observations
paragraphs: The TWIP mechanism has been confirmed for steels of similar chemical composition to the tested steel. They have the stacking fault energy values in the range 20 to 45 mJ/m 2  [ 11 ,  41 ,  42 – 43 ]. According to thermodynamic calculations based on the chemical composition, the tested steel has the SFE value of 24.6 mJ/m 2 . The microstructure investigation results confirmed that the steel studied belongs to the group of manganese steels hardened by mechanical twinning. Mechanical twins can be observed in every specimen subjected to tensile deformation, regardless of the strain rate applied (Fig.  20 ). Irrespective of the observation area within the individual specimen, no significant differences were revealed using the LM technique in the morphology and also in the qualitative assessment of the mechanical twins present in the microstructure. However, some differences are noted in the microstructure of the specimens deformed at various strain rates. In steel deformed in the static range of the strain rate (Fig.  20 a and b), austenite grains are observed to be somewhat elongated in the tensile direction, within which twins are generally formed in one twinning system. For these conditions, twinning rarely occurs in two twinning systems, and if it does, it covers smaller areas of grain (Fig.  20 b). A markedly increased twinning effect can be seen in dynamically tensioned steel with a pronounced grain elongation along the tension direction (Fig.  20  c ÷ f). Such results are in line with studies conducted in the works of [ 11 ,  16 ,  36 ]. Fig. 20 Microstructure of tested steel after tensile tests:  a  the area closer to the fracture, έ mean  = 0.001 s −1 ;  b  the area farther from the fracture, έ mean  = 0.001 s −1 ;  c  the area closer to the fracture, έ mean  = 300 s −1 ;  d  the area farther from the fracture, έ mean  = 300 s −1 ;  e  the area closer to the fracture, έ mean  = 950 s −1 ;  f  the area farther from the fracture, έ mean  = 950 s −1

It is also noticeable that in the area closer to the fracture (ca. 1.5 mm from the fracture) both the proportion of twins and their appearance more frequently in the two twinning systems is slightly higher compared to the zone about 4 mm away from the fracture (Fig.  20  c,d and Fig.  20  e,f).

Analyses of the results obtained for steels hardened by twinning in dynamic tensile experiments and the microstructural analyses complementing them can be discussed with reference to the work carried out in this area [ 6 ,  11 ,  14 ,  16 ,  20 ,  22 ,  36 ,  37 – 38 ,  44 ,  45 – 46 ]. However, each of these works assesses properties and microstructures that are similar in terms of mechanism but different in terms of chemical composition and therefore different SFE values.

As can be seen, many papers analyse the behaviour of TWIP steels in static and dynamic tension or compression tests on the basis of curves that approximate the direct results read from experimental measurements. For most of these results, one notices the regularity that the hardening exponent is lower for steels tested under dynamic conditions compared to the same steels tested under static conditions. The course of the  σ-ε  curve is characterised by a more rapid increase in stress with strain under static conditions [ 11 ,  36 ,  44 ]. This behaviour of austenitic steels, including TWIP steels, can be linked to the temperature factor and, strictly speaking, to the conversion of the plastic deformation work into heat which was the subject of research in the works [ 34 ,  47 ,  48 – 49 ]. It is known that during the plastic deformation process, part of the mechanical energy supplied is stored in the material structure as internal energy, while the remainder is dissipated as heat ( Q ). From both a cognitive and practical point of view, it is crucial to determine what percentage of the total strain energy ( E ) is converted into heat and what percentage remains in the material as internal energy, as described by the Taylor–Quinney coefficient ( β  =  Q/E ).

In experimental studies by [ 34 ,  49 ], the tensile behaviour of thin flat specimens was analysed. The relatively small thickness of these specimens enables efficient heat dissipation. In contradistinction, the cylindrical specimens examined in the present study are distinguished by a comparatively large diameter, which hinders effective heat transfer. Consequently, the generated heat is retained in the material for an extended duration, resulting in increased thermal accumulation during deformation. In practice, the lower the proportion of stored energy, the greater the amount of mechanical energy is converted directly into heat, leading to significant increases in material temperature during deformation. Under static deformation conditions where the strain rate is low and very low, the temperature of the material can rise to ca. 100°C [ 34 ]. For high strain rates, i.e. during a dynamic tensile test, the temperature of a material can rise up to 300°C, which significantly affects its microstructure and mechanical properties. This effect is particularly intensified for the cylindrical specimens studied in the work presented here, compared to the flat specimens studied so far [ 30 ]. In the case of TWIP steels, such a rapid rise in temperature can lead to a reduction in strain hardening exponent  n  which is confirmed by the results of the author’s own research presented in this paper. Furthermore, it is known that an increase in temperature, particularly during the deformation of TWIP steels, can alter the SFE value and thus change the predominant deformation mechanism, affecting the mechanical properties [ 50 ,  51 – 52 ]. Studies in this area are being intensively carried out but there is still a research gap, which the authors of this publication plan to fill in future scientific papers.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: The step-by-step methodology proposed in this paper, from force–time signal processing to determination of the true stress–true strain diagrams to approximation curve fitting, provides a sound experimental and computational basis for assessing the dynamic response of a material subjected to deformation at the very high strain rate range (from 10 2  up to 10 3  s −1 ) on the flywheel machine. The approach presented herein ensures the comparability of different test configurations and steel grades, particularly in the context of assessing energy absorption potential. The experimental  σ true -ε true  curves determined from signals recorded during dynamic tensile tests on cylindrical specimens using the flywheel machine, demonstrated oscillations as a consequence of elastic stress wave propagation effects in the stand construction. The oscillations were corrected using a power approximation function assuming a constant  n  value. This resulted in generation of continuous and physically representative flow curves at varying strain rates. The experimental conditions applied in this study resulted in the observed sensitivity of the tested steel to strain rate, as evidenced by the calculated increase in flow stress. The values of absorbed energy by the tested steel, both in relation to unit volume (VEA) and unit mass (SEA), exhibited an increase in accordance with an increase in strain rate. A comparative analysis of the steel under scrutiny with other TWIP steels exhibiting analogous carbon content reveals that it demonstrates comparable or higher absorbed energy and significantly higher VEA and SEA values in comparison to DP600 steel, which is commonly utilised in automotive energy-absorbing structural components. A thorough analysis and comparison of the strain-hardening behaviour for the tested steel under both static and dynamic deformation conditions, as well as for other TWIP steels, was conducted. This analysis revealed a reduction in the hardening rate under dynamic conditions in comparison to static tests. This phenomenon is attributed to the process of energy dispersion, which occurs as a result of its conversion to heat. In the TWIP steel examined in the dynamic tests conducted on cylindrical specimens, the majority of the mechanical energy is directly converted into heat. This process does not result in significant dissipation, but rather, the energy accumulates, making the process essentially adiabatic. Metallographic investigations confirmed that mechanical twinning is the predominant deformation mechanism in the steel studied, with increased twinning density and multisystem twinning under dynamic conditions.
